betterCitation: Natalia Ginzburg, The Little Virtues, Winter in the Abruzzi, the closing sentence (trans. Dick Davis, 1985, Arcade text of 2017)
reason: The line survives, but the citation needs one correction, and it is the correction this track exists to catch. WORDING: I fetched the Salon reprint raw rather than through a summariser, because the summariser answered twice and contradicted itself, once saying the piece prints 'forever' and 'realize' and once saying it is British throughout with 'for ever' and 'realise'. The raw page settles it: the essay ends 'At that time I believed in a simple and happy future, rich with hopes that were fulfilled, with experiences and plans that were shared. But that was the best time of my life, and only now that it has gone from me forever-only now do I realize it', with an em dash closed up, 'forever' as one word and 'realize' with a z, and 'realize' used twice more earlier in the same paragraph. So the proposed quotation is verbatim in the printing that was read, the preceding sentence is the one the locator names, and it is the closing sentence of the essay as claimed. THE CORRECTION: the printing that was read is the Arcade Publishing reissue of 2017, which Salon credits, and its spelling is Americanised. Dick Davis's translation was first published by Carcanet in Manchester in 1985, and a British house setting a British translator in 1985 would very plausibly print 'for ever' and 'realise'. Nobody has opened the Carcanet text; the only printing on the Internet Archive is the Arcade one, and it is lending restricted. So the source line as it stands names 1985 while carrying 2017 accidentals, which is precisely the mismatch rule 4 is written against. The fix is not to drop the line but to name the printing whose wording it uses: 'Natalia Ginzburg, The Little Virtues, Winter in the Abruzzi, the closing sentence (trans. Dick Davis, 1985, Arcade text of 2017)', 128 characters, still under the cap, still leading with the name and carrying no dash. ATTRIBUTION: Ginzburg's own essay, Inverno in Abruzzo of 1944, collected in Le piccole virtu, 1962; Davis is the named translator and the only English translator of the collection, so this is not a case of another translator's wording travelling under his name. Not on the misattribution list. SCOPE AND SHAPE: well before 1999, essay, prose as prose, ends in a full stop, no straight double quote; the em dash sits inside the quotation, where it is the author's punctuation, not in the source or the note, so rule 5 is untouched. PUBLISHABILITY: the sentence before it in the essay reports her husband's death in prison, but the quotation itself carries none of that and needs no warning. shipped.js: not shipped, no near match, Natalia Ginzburg at 1 of 3 (May), not banned, once only in August.
